newsitem.title: FIJI: Fiji upper house passes non-racial constitution.
newsitem.headline: Fiji upper house passes non-racial constitution.

text.p: Fiji's upper house of parliament, the Senate, on Thursday passed a law to change the South Pacific nation's constitution to end the guaranteed parliamentary dominance by native Fijians.
The reform reduces the number of House of Representative seats reserved for ethnic Fijians to 23 in an expanded 71 seat lower house from 37 in the current 70-seat chamber.
The bill -- due to be enacted by President Ratu Sir Kamisese Mara soon and to apply in time for the next election in 1999 -- was approved by all 31 senators present for the vote.
Under the amended constitution, the new 71-seat parliament will see 23 Fijian seats, 19 Indian seats, three for mixed races, one for Rotuma Islanders and 25 open seats for any race.
It will also open the way for a multi-racial government and permit a non-indigenous Fijian to become prime minister.
The racially biased constitution was introduced to prevent Fiji's Indian population from re-gaining political control after two military coups in 1987.

Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka, who as an army officer led the 1987 coups that overthrew the then Indian-dominated government, has said he would be seeking a multi-racial cabinet under the new constitution.
The former constitution, introduced in 1990 by Rabuka, gave Fijians 37 seats in parliament, reserved 27 seats for Indians and split the remaining six between mixed-race politicians and Rotumans.

Indians, who were brought to Fiji at the turn of the century to work on sugar plantations, now make up 45 percent of the country's 750,000-strong population and are influential in the business community.
In a statement issued in Cairns, Australian Foreign Minister Alexander Downer welcomed the reform as offering new hope to Fijians.
"The new constitution provides a political and social framework within which all Fiji's communities can realise their individual and collective aspirations," he said.
"It provides a new base from which Fiji can begin to move to fulfil its undoubted economic and social potential," he said.
